title: Predictable Account Password Generation for OAuth Users
description: When an OAuth login occurs, the application creates or updates local user accounts using a password that is deterministically computed from the user's email address by reversing the email string and base64-encoding it (`btoa(profile.email.split('').reverse().join(''))`). Because email addresses are public or discoverable, an attacker can compute the account password for any OAuth user and log into their account using the standard login interface, leading to full account takeover and OAuth authentication bypass.

Evaluating 16-digit credit card numbers as IEEE 754 floating-point numbers causes integer precision loss, causing invalid credit card numbers to pass validation or corrupting card digits prior to transmission.

The endpoint fetches the basket via BasketModel.findByPk(id) and updates it without checking whether the requesting user owns the basket or possesses appropriate permissions, allowing unauthorized callers to manipulate arbitrary users' baskets.

Additionally, if basketIds[0] is omitted or user session is missing, the authorization check is bypassed entirely. This allows an attacker to add items to arbitrary user baskets by supplying multiple BasketId entries or manipulating parameter structures.

description: The verifySync function from otplib is invoked with an epochTolerance of 30 during TOTP verification (line 31) and setup (line 118). This significantly degrades the security of multi-factor authentication and facilitates token replay and brute-force attacks.

title: Directory Traversal in Quarantine File Handler
description: The serveQuarantineFiles handler accepts a user-controlled `file` parameter and attempts to prevent directory traversal by checking if it contains forward slashes (`!file.includes('/')`). This validation is insufficient because inputs such as `..` (without a slash) or backslashes on Windows platforms (e.g., `..\`) bypass the check. Consequently, `path.resolve('ftp/quarantine/', file)` can resolve to files outside the intended quarantine directory, allowing arbitrary file reading.

trace.description: The serveQuarantineFiles route handler receives user input via request parameters.
User input from params.file is assigned to the local variable file.
Flawed design check only verifies that forward slashes are absent, failing to block '..' path traversal sequences or backslashes.
path.resolve evaluates the relative path traversal input and res.sendFile returns the target file from the filesystem.

title: Broken Object Level Authorization (BOLA) in Order Placement
description: The order placement endpoint /rest/basket/:id/checkout accepts a basket ID as a path parameter and completes checkout for that basket without verifying whether the target basket belongs to the authenticated user. An attacker can pass any basket ID to checkout and clear another user's shopping basket.

BasketModel.findOne fetches the basket matching the provided ID without scoping the query to the authenticated user.
The found basket promise resolves and control passes to the asynchronous callback.
Verification passes checking that the basket object exists in database.
Basket coupon is cleared without user ownership verification.
Order confirmation response with order ID is returned to caller.
Basket items are deleted and order confirmation is generated for the unvalidated basket.

title: User-Controlled UserId in Request Body for Wallet Balance Operations
description: When processing wallet payments or awarding bonus points during order placement, the handler relies on req.body.UserId supplied by the caller rather than the authenticated session identity. An attacker can supply another user's ID to charge their wallet balance or credit bonus points to an arbitrary account.

Checks if orderDetails exists and paymentId equals 'wallet'.
Verifies target user wallet exists and balance is sufficient for order.
Bonus points are credited to the target user account specified in req.body.UserId.

title: Unauthenticated Base64 Coupon Validation Permitting Discount Forgery
description: The calculateApplicableDiscount function parses user-supplied base64 encoded coupon data from req.body.couponData into a campaign code and validOn timestamp. Because base64 is an encoding scheme without cryptographic signatures or HMAC verification, any caller can construct coupon strings for static campaign codes and claim discounts up to 75% without possessing a valid issued coupon.

Extracts couponDate timestamp from the split base64 payload.
Looks up matching campaign from static campaigns dictionary.
Decoded campaign code and date match campaign defaults and forged discount percentage is returned.
Decoded campaign code and date are matched against campaign defaults and discount is applied.

title: Broken Object Level Authorization in getPaymentMethods
description: The getPaymentMethods route relies on req.body.UserId to filter payment cards. When req.body.UserId is undefined or manipulated by an attacker, Sequelize ignores the undefined filter property and executes a query without the UserId constraint (CardModel.findAll({ where: { UserId: undefined } })), returning payment methods belonging to all users across the application.

CardModel.findAll queries the database without validating that req.body.UserId matches the authenticated user or exists.

title: Broken Object Level Authorization in getPaymentMethodById
description: The getPaymentMethodById route handler fetches card details using CardModel.findOne matching id: req.params.id and UserId: req.body.UserId. If req.body.UserId is omitted or controlled by the attacker, Sequelize drops the UserId filter condition, allowing any caller to retrieve payment card details belonging to any user by specifying their card ID.

req.params.id and req.body.UserId are passed into the database query criteria.
CardModel.findOne fetches the card without proper server-side ownership authorization check.

title: Broken Object Level Authorization in delPaymentMethodById
description: The delPaymentMethodById handler deletes a card record using CardModel.destroy with where clause containing id: req.params.id and UserId: req.body.UserId. If req.body.UserId is undefined or supplied by the client, the ownership check is bypassed, permitting an attacker to delete any payment card record by ID.

req.params.id and req.body.UserId are passed to CardModel.destroy.
CardModel.destroy executes deletion without validating resource ownership against session context.

title: SQL Injection in getRecycleItem via JSON.parse on Path Parameter
description: The getRecycleItem endpoint parses the route parameter req.params.id using JSON.parse and passes the resulting object directly into Sequelize's RecycleModel.findAll query where clause. An attacker can supply a JSON payload with SQL injection structures or ORM operators, bypassing type safety and injecting arbitrary SQL commands into the database query.

title: Unauthenticated Notification Re-triggering and Lack of Rate Limiting
description: The `repeatNotification` handler allows any caller to pass a `challenge` parameter and re-trigger challenge completion notifications via `challengeUtils.sendNotification`. The route performs no authentication or user authorization checks to verify whether the requester is permitted to trigger system notifications. Furthermore, the endpoint lacks rate-limiting controls, allowing unauthenticated attackers to repeatedly invoke notification triggers and generate excessive websocket/push notification traffic.

Decodes the caller-controlled challenge parameter string.
Retrieves challenge record by name without checking request credentials or session authorization.
Evaluates whether the retrieved challenge object is present and solved.
Executes sendNotification for solved challenge without authorization or rate-limiting checks.

title: Stored Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) via True-Client-IP Header
description: The route handler extracts the `True-Client-IP` header directly from incoming requests. When the `httpHeaderXssChallenge` is enabled, sanitization of `lastLoginIp` is explicitly bypassed, allowing untrusted HTTP header values to be persisted directly into the user record in the database. When this IP address is later rendered in frontend views or administrative dashboards without proper context-aware escaping, malicious HTML/JavaScript payloads in the header execute in the browser context.

The code checks whether `lastLoginIp` is an array of header values.
The code checks if `lastLoginIp` is undefined, leaving the header payload untouched if present.
The authenticated user record is fetched from the database via `UserModel.findByPk(loggedInUser.data.id)`.
The un-sanitized `lastLoginIp` string is saved to the database via `user?.update({ lastLoginIp: ... })`, creating a stored injection/XSS vulnerability.

title: Unauthenticated Wallet NFT Verification and Lack of Cryptographic Ownership Proof
description: The walletNFTVerify endpoint accepts any Ethereum address via req.body.walletAddress without requiring cryptographic signature verification (such as a signed message/nonce) or checking whether the address belongs to the authenticated user. An attacker can supply any target wallet address that has minted an NFT to bypass ownership verification, consume the mint status from the server's tracking set, or solve the challenge on behalf of another user.

The request handler function executes with caller-supplied Express request object req.

The endpoint responds with HTTP 200 and marks the challenge as solved without verifying wallet ownership or user session.
The handler checks addressesMinted.has(metamaskAddress) and deletes the address, allowing an attacker to verify any wallet address without ownership proof.

title: Unbounded In-Memory Set for Minted NFT Addresses
description: The NFT listener appends all observed minter addresses into a global addressesMinted Set when contract events fire. Because there is no maximum size limit or time-to-live eviction mechanism, unclaimed or maliciously spammed mint events can cause the Set to grow indefinitely, leading to high memory consumption and potential denial of service.

When the contract emits NFTMinted events, minter address strings are passed into the callback function.
The nftMintListener function is exported to set up the Web3 event listener route handler.
The handler checks if the minter address is already present in addressesMinted.
minter addresses are added to the global addressesMinted Set without any upper capacity limit or cleanup policy.

title: Stored Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) via Unsanitized SVG Profile Image Upload
description: The profile image upload endpoint validates files by checking if the MIME type detected by file-type starts with 'image/'. This check permits image types such as SVG ('image/svg+xml') which can contain arbitrary inline JavaScript markup. The application writes the unformatted file buffer directly into a public directory and updates the user record profile image path without sanitizing or restricting dangerous file formats. When rendered in a client browser, any embedded scripts in the uploaded SVG execute in the context of the victim's session.

The raw image buffer is written directly to the public assets upload folder.

title: Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) via profile image URL upload
description: The route handler accepts a user-provided URL (req.body.imageUrl) and performs an HTTP GET request using fetch(url) without validating the scheme, host, or IP address. An attacker can supply internal network URLs or cloud metadata endpoints to read private resources or interact with internal APIs.

description: When fetching the image URL fails, the application stores the raw user-controlled imageUrl directly in the user's profileImage field in the database without validating the scheme or sanitizing the URL string. An attacker can supply payloads using JavaScript URI schemes (e.g., javascript:alert(1)), leading to Stored XSS when rendered in client browsers.

title: Broken Object-Level Authorization (BOLA) via Obfuscated Email Collisions in Order History Lookup
description: In `orderHistory()`, the authenticated user's email address is retrieved from their session token and modified by replacing all vowels with asterisks (`*`). The database query then fetches order records using this modified string (`updatedEmail`). Because replacing vowels with asterisks creates collisions between distinct email addresses (e.g. `user1@test.com` and `user2@tast.com`), a user can view order histories belonging to other users whose email addresses produce identical obfuscated strings. This breaks per-user object-level authorization.

trace.description: The orderHistory request handler receives an HTTP request on GET /rest/order-history.
Authenticated user session data is retrieved from security.authenticatedUsers using the Bearer token.
The user's email is obfuscated by replacing all vowels with '*' characters, creating potential collisions across user accounts.
The handler checks if the authenticated user object contains email and id properties.
The email address string is extracted from loggedInUser.data.email.
ordersCollection.find is called with the collision-prone obfuscated email, returning orders belonging to multiple users.

title: Unrestricted Resource Consumption via Unpaginated Order Retrieval in allOrders
description: In `allOrders()`, `ordersCollection.find()` is called without any query parameters, limits, or pagination constraints. The handler loads all order documents present in the database into memory, reverses the array, and returns them in the response. As the database grows, calling this endpoint can exhaust server memory and CPU, leading to denial of service.

trace.description: The allOrders request handler receives an HTTP GET request on /rest/order-history/orders.
The entire unpaginated order list is reversed in memory and returned as a JSON response, leading to server memory exhaustion.
ordersCollection.find() fetches the entire order history collection without pagination limits or constraints.

title: Hardcoded Hashids Salt Enables Continue Code Forgery and Unauthorized Challenge Solving
description: The restoreProgress, restoreProgressFindIt, and restoreProgressFixIt endpoint handlers rely on Hashids with hardcoded salt strings ('this is my salt', 'this is the salt for findIt challenges', 'yet another salt for the fixIt challenges') to encode and decode user progress state. Because the salts are static and embedded in the source code, attackers can locally construct valid continue codes encoding arbitrary challenge IDs and submit them to the unauthenticated endpoints to force the server to solve challenges without authorization.

title: SQL Injection in Product Search Query
description: The searchProducts handler extracts the query parameter 'q' from the request query string and directly interpolates it into a raw SQL query string passed to `models.sequelize.query`. Truncating the query parameter length to 200 characters does not prevent SQL injection attacks, allowing an unauthenticated attacker to manipulate the query structure, bypass intended filters, or extract arbitrary data from the database.

The `criteria` variable is capped at 200 characters, which does not sanitize or escape SQL metacharacters.
`models.sequelize.query` executes a raw SQL query built using string interpolation of untrusted `criteria`.

title: Reflected Cross-Site Scripting via Unsanitized Error Message in Redirect Handler
description: In `performRedirect`, when `security.isRedirectAllowed(toUrl)` returns false, the unvalidated `toUrl` input from `req.query.to` is directly concatenated into an Error object message: `new Error('Unrecognized target URL for redirect: ' + toUrl)`. Passing untrusted user input directly into an error passed to `next()` can result in reflected cross-site scripting (XSS) or HTML injection if the error handler renders error messages without proper HTML output encoding.

The `toUrl` string is checked against `security.isRedirectAllowed(toUrl)`, evaluating to false for unrecognized targets.
When authorization fails, execution moves to the else block setting HTTP status 406.
`toUrl` is concatenated into an `Error` object and passed to `next()`, causing untrusted input to reach the response rendering sink unencoded.

title: Unvalidated Redirection (Open Redirect) in Redirection Handler
description: The `performRedirect` handler fetches `to` from request query parameters and issues an HTTP redirect via `res.redirect(toUrl)`. Relying on permissive or bypassable allowlist rules enables malicious actors to craft redirect links that send users to phishing or malware hosting sites under the trust of the application's domain.

`toUrl` is validated by `security.isRedirectAllowed(toUrl)`.

title: Flawed Prefix Validation in Redirect Allowlist Checking
description: The `isUnintendedRedirect` function validates target URLs using prefix matching via `utils.startsWith(toUrl, allowedUrl)`. Simple prefix matching without enforcing URL domain boundaries permits domain spoofing bypasses (e.g., `https://allowed-domain.com.attacker.com` or `https://allowed-domain.com@attacker.com`), rendering the redirect allowlist ineffective.

title: Unauthenticated Account Enumeration and Security Question Exposure via Undefined Filter Handling
description: The securityQuestion route handler accepts an optional email query parameter to retrieve the user's registered security question. The response explicitly reveals whether an account exists by returning `{ question }` when found versus `{}` when not found, permitting user account enumeration. Furthermore, if the email parameter is omitted or undefined, `email?.toString()` evaluates to `undefined`. In Sequelize, passing `{ email: undefined }` inside a where object causes the filter to be omitted (`where: {}`), causing the query to match the first security answer in the database and leak its associated security question.

The route returns the security question in JSON format, enabling account enumeration and unauthorized disclosure of security questions.

The endpoint lacks rate limiting, throttling, or account lockout mechanisms after failed attempts. An attacker can perform automated brute-force attacks against security answers to reset arbitrary user passwords.

description: The showProductReviews handler constructs a MongoDB query by string-concatenating the user-controlled route parameter req.params.id directly into a $where JavaScript expression. When noSqlCommandChallenge is active, this allows callers to inject arbitrary JavaScript code into the MongoDB query engine context.

An attacker can inject arbitrary JavaScript code into the MongoDB $where query clause, leading to NoSQL injection and potential server-side code execution within the database engine.

title: Unbounded Array Memory Growth in captchaBypassChallenge Middleware
description: The `captchaBypassChallenge` middleware stores timestamp entries in `req.app.locals.captchaBypassReqTimes` array using `req.app.locals.captchaReqId` as the index and increments `captchaReqId` for every incoming request. Because there is no maximum limit, rotation, or cleanup mechanism applied to `captchaBypassReqTimes`, an attacker can repeatedly issue requests to routes protected by this middleware to cause uncontrolled memory growth in application locals, eventually leading to application instability or Denial of Service through process memory exhaustion.

title: Stored Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) via Unsanitized Profile Username
description: The profile update endpoint accepts `req.body.username` directly from user input and persists it into the database via `user.update()` without performing any HTML sanitization, character filtering, or output encoding validation. An attacker can submit malicious HTML or JavaScript markup as their username, which will be stored in the database and subsequently rendered in victim browsers whenever the username is displayed.

An attacker can supply a NoSQL query operator (e.g. { '$ne': null }) in 'req.body.id' which, combined with 'multi: true', allows modifying all product reviews in the database.

description: The getUserProfile endpoint retrieves the user's username and checks if it matches a pattern containing '#{...}'. If matched, it extracts the code within the pattern and passes it directly to JavaScript's eval() function, allowing an attacker who can set their username to execute arbitrary code on the server.

Furthermore, because `walletsConnected` is stored in memory without any size bounds or rate limiting, an attacker can make repeated HTTP requests with unique address values to continuously populate the Set, leading to uncontrolled memory consumption and potential application denial of service (OOM crash).

title: Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) via Unsanitized Subtitle Content Injection
description: In promotionVideo, subtitle content loaded from disk via getSubsFromFile() is directly concatenated into a raw inline <script> tag without HTML or script context encoding. If an attacker can influence the subtitle file contents or configuration, arbitrary JavaScript code will be executed in the browser of any user viewing the promotion page.

title: Unhandled Exception and Denial of Service via Malformed Range Header
description: The getVideo route handler parses the client-provided HTTP Range header using parseInt without validating if the resulting offset values are valid numbers or non-negative integers. Malformed Range headers (e.g. bytes=-100 or non-numeric values) produce NaN for start or end parameters passed to fs.createReadStream, throwing an unhandled exception that can crash the server process or abort connection handling.
